extracted.intended_audience: journalists, newsroom editors, media scholars, and journalism students
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing the values, opinions, reality judgments, and organizational dynamics that govern news selection and production in mainstream newsrooms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enduring values
rubrics_metrics.description: The recurring, profession-level values built into importance judgments (e.g., social order, responsible capitalism, individualism, moderation, pastoralism, leadership) that make objectivity possible and routinely enter news selection unconsciously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enduring values are part of journalism rather than individual journalists; they operate unconsciously through importance judgments and are applied variably across organizations. Examples: press emphasis on social order, suspicion of grand plans, praise for competent leadership. They both enable the profession's self-image of objectivity and constrain which stories are considered newsworthy (and which structural critiques are less likely to appear).

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance judgments / news judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions about what is 'important' and therefore newsworthy—these foundational judgments guide story selection and implicitly carry values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Importance judgments combine considerations of source suitability and enduring values; they determine whether events are noticed and reported. They are selective, time- and resource-limited, and vary by journalist and organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conscious opinions — Taking stands
rubrics_metrics.description: Topical or story-specific opinions and explicit stands that newsmagazines and journalists take; these are often formulated by writers but reflect or are approved by top editors or executives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magazines may compete by taking stands; consistency is managed through a 'voice' or 'attitude.' Top editors often determine major stands; executives may formulate firm opinion. Television avoids explicit editorial positions but nonetheless expresses opinions through nightly presentation and anchors/commentators. Stands can be shaped by institutional leadership and persist because journalists fear inconsistency charges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unconscious opinions (connotative language)
rubrics_metrics.description: Opinions that enter reporting unintentionally through connotative or pejorative word choices (e.g., describing participants as 'mobs' or using sardonic tones), shared enough to be taken for granted until they become controversial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These opinions are pervasive and only become visible when criticized; they can be moderated or abandoned after peer or public critique (e.g., reduction of sexist terminology after protests).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reality judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Assumptions about external reality embedded in the concepts journalists use to grasp events (decisions about what is new vs. old, normal vs. abnormal), often manifesting as stereotypes or taken-for-granted models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reality judgments shape how phenomena are framed (e.g., seeing Vietnam as an international Cold War conflict rather than a civil war). They derive from journalists' collective mental pictures of nation and society and can exclude alternative perspectives (e.g., poor people's views). Stereotypes are commonly borrowed for availability and familiarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideological editing
rubrics_metrics.description: The (rare) practice by which ideological considerations enter story selection or production—stories can be killed or toned down for ideological reasons, but ideological conclusions typically survive only if supported by evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a Time story was killed because it 'made the Communists look too good.' More often, ideological editing occurs during production when editors soften writers' strong opinions; seniority and writer skill can mitigate editorial interference. Evidence-based conclusions are more likely to be left intact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paraideology (journalistic paraideology)
rubrics_metrics.description: The composite of enduring values, conscious and unconscious opinions, and reality judgments that functions like an implicit ideology within journalism—taken as non-ideological by its adherents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paraideology originates in workplace and profession-level norms; it is flexible but shaped toward homogeneity by conformity pressures and by top editors' more conservative tendencies. It informs news judgment and is politically and culturally slanted without being perceived as ideology by practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of seniority and trust in editorial autonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Senior, trusted journalists and reporters are granted more autonomy and latitude to present conclusions or to choose subject matter; their reputations influence whether opinions are allowed to stand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Senior reporters who have long covered beats are trusted to choose filming and framing; top producers/editors may accept their conclusions if supported by evidence. Conversely, less senior or ideologically labeled staff may be curtailed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience mediation of stands
rubrics_metrics.description: The shaping of editorial stands and expressed opinions by perceived public mood and audience concerns; decisions are influenced by estimations of what the national audience will accept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and producers often couch opinions as reflecting the audience or 'public mood.' National programs avoid taking positions that might alienate significant portions of their audience; local differences (e.g., Atlanta vs. Chicago) influence nuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work requirements and source efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical newsroom working conditions that favor regular, productive sources (e.g., the president) and thereby influence story selection and framing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists argue that operational needs (accessibility, productivity) drive coverage choices; however, these practical drivers interact with enduring values to shape outcomes (e.g., favoring leaders because they are efficient sources, not purely out of value for leadership).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conformity pressures and the house radical/house conservative dynamic
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal labeling of staff as 'house radicals' or 'house conservatives' functions to set ideological boundaries, allow others to feel ideology-neutral, and regulate acceptable opinion within the newsroom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: House radicals (often younger, different lifestyles) tended to be marginalized and left; house conservatives (usually older writers/editors) persisted and served as boundary markers. Labels enable colleagues to view themselves as objective and help police extremes on either side.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value insertion via factual reporting (researchers/reporters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers and reporters, by adding factual details, can more successfully insert ideological points because facts are harder to contest than explicit ideas; editors may still delete such facts for length or content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invisible ideologists often work as researchers/reporters and use factual additions to convey perspectives; debate with editors is constrained by reputational costs and the risk of being seen as a 'crank.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Opinion change dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalistic opinions (conscious or unconscious) tend to change mainly in response to highly visible, traumatic events and to intraprofessional processes of peer opinion change; journalists resist changing stands otherwise to avoid charges of inconsistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: shifts in coverage of the Vietnam War after the Tet offensive; change often follows accumulation of less visible events and peer-reviewed reporting. Unconscious opinions may become conscious following criticism and then be altered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enduring values' alignment with Progressive origins and business interests
rubrics_metrics.description: The enduring values resemble Progressive-era reformist values and align with the interests of political rhetoric and corporate sponsors, making certain kinds of systemic critique less likely in news coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical ties to Progressivism explain the prominence of exposure and reform themes in journalism. Because enduring values coincide with broader political rhetoric and business interests, coverage tends to privilege responsible-capitalism narratives and treat systemic faults as 'bad apples' rather than structural.

rubrics_metrics.name: Values derived from working conditions (instrumental origins)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some journalistic values (e.g., support for civil liberties, antipathy to bureaucracy, emphasis on responsible leadership, moderatism) stem from journalists' organizational positions and practical necessities rather than purely normative commitments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civil liberties are valued instrumentally because journalistic autonomy depends on freedom of the press; anti-bureaucracy may derive from journalists' discomfort within organizations; moderatism functions defensively to avoid sustained criticism and to maintain work pace.
